extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, in-house counsel, policy makers, and stakeholders interested in the America Invents Act and its implementation
extracted.subtask_description: Legislative-history and practitioner-oriented explanation of key America Invents Act (AIA) provisions affecting patentability, defenses, post-grant review, and PTO administration, with examples and intended scope of several sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of control for PCU defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of 'control' (power to govern) for purposes of the PCU defense: 'direct or indirect power to govern the management and policies of a person or entity, whether through ownership of securities, by contract, or otherwise; the power or authority to manage, direct, or oversee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine when one entity effectively controls another for defense purposes—includes indirect means such as contracts or ownership; examples and boundary-drawing implied by the words 'direct or indirect.'

rubrics_metrics.name: University exception extended to tech-transfer organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (e)(5)(A), the university exception, is extended to include university technology-transfer organizations (e.g., Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities and their technology-transfer organizations may qualify for the university exception; an exception-to-the-exception (subparagraph (B)) applies only when the federal government is affirmatively prohibited (by statute, regulation, or executive order) from funding the research activity in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment and periodic/seasonal use
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (e)(4) bars assertion of the defense if use of the subject matter has been abandoned, but should not be construed to require continuous use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some subject matter is inherently used only periodically or seasonally; if so used, its use is not 'abandoned.' The interpretation should account for periodic/seasonal uses as non-abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period and 'available to the public' standard (Section 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct interpretation: an action bars under new 102(a) only if it makes the patented subject matter 'available to the public' before the effective filing date; if an action triggers 102(a) it inherently triggers the grace period in section 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inclusion of 'or otherwise available to the public' in 102(a) limits prior-art events to those that make the invention public. Public uses and sales are prior art only if they make the invention available to the public; nondisclosing uses or secret sales that do not make the invention available to the public should not be treated as prior art outside the grace period. The committee reports and sponsors' statements are cited as consistent support for this interpretive stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-mode requirement precluded as basis for cancellation (Section 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 15 precludes the use of the best-mode requirement as a basis for cancelling a claim or holding it invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Act, allegations that an inventor failed to disclose the best mode cannot be used to invalidate or cancel claims—i.e., best-mode is no longer a ground for post-issuance challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery allowed in derivation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery is allowed in derivation proceedings created by the Act because Section 24 of title 35 allows discovery in any 'contested case' and Patent Office regulations (37 CFR 41.2(2)) indicate contested cases include Board proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation proceedings are 'contested cases' and thus the standard discovery tools applicable to contested agency proceedings are available; nothing in the Act or regulations suggests discovery would be disallowed in derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological-invention exclusion to Section 18 (business-method review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 excludes 'technological inventions' from the business-method review program. Technological inventions are those whose novelty turns on a technological innovation over the prior art and that solve a technical problem with a technical solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exclusion does not apply merely because a patent 'recites technology.' A patent must be novel as technology (e.g., novelty rests on a technical innovation). Mechanical or manufacturing inventions whose novelty is technological (e.g., machines that count/sort/authenticate currency) are excluded. The PTO should construe the regulatory implementation of the exclusion with this understanding so that legitimate technological patents are not subject to Section 18 review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of software elements under Section 18
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents that recite software elements are not automatically ineligible for Section 18 review; they are excluded only if the invention is 'novel as software' (i.e., a true software/technological invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim merely includes software elements but does not assert novelty as software or does not colorably appear novel as software, it is not excluded from review solely on that basis. By contrast, an actual software invention whose novelty is technological falls within the 'technological invention' exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'covered business method patent' and financial-product nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'covered business method patent' is one that relates to a financial product or service or to performing data processing/operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be eligible for Section 18 review the patent claims must be broad enough to cover a financial product or service. 'Financial product or service' is given a broad nonexclusive list of examples (extending credit, servicing loans, leasing, real estate services, payment instruments, check processing, financial data processing, benefits administration, fraud detection, financial advisory/management consulting, securities transactions, insurance, consumer reports, asset management, trust functions, annuities, brokerage, etc.). The provision covers patents claiming activities that are financial in nature, incidental to, or complementary to financial activities—claims need not recite a specific financial product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 18 standing/privy expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: The House amendment expanded standing to permit filing a Section 18 petition when a 'privy' of the petitioner has been sued or accused of infringement; a 'privy' has a direct relationship to the petitioner with respect to the allegedly infringing product or service (effectively customers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The addition of 'privy' demonstrates that Section 18 is intended to be used by a wide range of petitioners, including those whose customers face suits; it is not limited to actors within the financial services industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 14: ban on tax patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 14 bans tax patents, ending the practice of obtaining patents for tax avoidance strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ban halts new and pending tax patent applications. The provision is intended to be narrowly construed so that software that merely helps taxpayers prepare returns may still be patentable, but the ban is not intended to authorize patents on business methods or financial management software generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 22: PTO fee funding and fee-setting authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 22 helps ensure that fees collected by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office fund the Office and its administration of the patent system, addressing fee diversion and allowing PTO to better hire examiners and reduce backlog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dedicating user fees to PTO operations is presented as necessary to improve pendency, reduce backlog, and improve patent quality. The committee/coalition letters urge retention of fee-setting/dedication provisions to address the ~1.2 million application backlog and three-year pendency problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 16: false marking reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 16 reforms false marking claims to end frivolous suits while preserving rights for those who suffered actual harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legislation seeks to prevent abusive false-marking litigation but retain remedies for parties who can demonstrate concrete injury from false marking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5: prior user rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 creates a prior user right protecting parties who first commercially use an invention, thereby protecting manufacturers and giving incentives for domestic production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior commercial users gain a defense against later patentees; the provision is framed as protecting rights of early users and encouraging manufacturing in the U.S., while also 'fully protecting' universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 19: restriction on joinder of defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 19 restricts joinder of defendants in patent infringement suits when their connection to the underlying disputes is tenuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to curb litigation abuses by preventing overly broad joinder of unrelated defendants in patent suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO Ombudsman, small-entity supports, and satellite office
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act establishes a USPTO Ombudsman Program to assist small businesses with patent filing issues, provides reduced fees for micro entities and small businesses, and authorizes a satellite PTO office (e.g., in Detroit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These administrative reforms are intended to help small firms navigate patent bureaucracy, reduce costs for small/micro entities, modernize the PTO, improve examiner hiring and efficiency, and bring PTO services closer to regional innovators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative intent and reliance on committee reports and sponsor statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and executive officials should rely on the Act's committee reports and sponsors' floor statements (e.g., Chairmen Smith and Leahy) for correct interpretation of Section 102 and other provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes consistent committee report language (2007 and 2011 reports) and sponsor floor remarks as authoritative interpretive aids; opponents failing to point to contrary caselaw are cautioned.
